description: I'm trying to build something to advance my career in the world of AI. This could be the beginning of a great team.
summary: NASA has tracked active fires from space for over two decades, but the record is split across sensors that count the same fires very differently. In Australia, VIIRS records about 4.3 times more detections than MODIS, so when a long record switches satellites, fire activity appears to jump several-fold even though nothing changed on the ground. Fire Pulse fixes this. A Python pipeline cleans and grids 4.47 million NASA FIRMS detections and rescales VIIRS to the MODIS baseline, first with a conversion factor for every 50 km square and then with a gradient-boosting machine-learning model. Tested on 2025, a year the models never saw, the error drops from 376% without harmonisation to 8.5%. An interactive web app turns the result into a burning-activity calendar where anyone can pick a region and see when its fire season starts, peaks and ends, and whether a year is unusual. We also ran a fair forecasting contest: six algorithms predicted 2026, their predictions were locked, and real 2026 NASA data picked the winner, which now forecasts 2027.
details:
Fire Pulse turns NASA’s satellite fire record into one consistent burning-activity calendar. Active-fire detections come from two sensors that count the same fires very differently: VIIRS has smaller pixels (375 m vs 1 km) and far better night-time sensitivity, so in Australia it records about 4.3 times more detections than MODIS. When a long record switches from one sensor to the other, fire activity appears to jump several-fold with nothing changing on the ground.

Our pipeline:

  1. Extracts NASA FIRMS archive data for Australia, 2023–2025: MODIS C6.1 (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS 375 m (NOAA-20), about 5 million records.
  2. Cleans it, keeping vegetation fires with nominal or high confidence (4.47 million detections).
  3. Grids detections into 0.5° squares (about 50 km) per day, per sensor.
  4. Harmonises VIIRS to the MODIS baseline in two ways: a conversion factor for every square, pulled toward the national factor where data is thin, and a gradient-boosting model that also uses fire radiative power, the day/night split, season and location.
  5. Validates by learning on 2023–2024 and testing on 2025. Weekly error falls from 376% with no harmonisation to 11.4% with the per-square factor and 8.5% with machine learning. Trained on 2023 alone, ML still wins (8.9% vs 12.2%).
  6. Forecasts: six algorithms predicted every month of 2026 using only 2023–2025. Their predictions were locked with a timestamp and SHA-256 fingerprint, then scored against real 2026 NASA data. The median of three years won (1.2% error on the January–October total) and now forecasts 2027.

The web app lets anyone pick a region on a map and see a daily burning calendar, when each fire season started, peaked and ended, whether a year is unusual, a plain-English summary, a raw-versus-harmonised comparison, the 2026 forecast leaderboard and a 2027 forecast with an 80% range.

What benefits does it have?

  • Fire and emergency crews: know when their region’s season usually starts and peaks, and staff up in time.
  • Land managers: schedule controlled burns outside peak weeks.
  • Scientists: a long fire record that no longer jumps when satellites change.
  • NASA: keeps 25 years of MODIS data comparable as missions retire. VIIRS S-NPP’s record ended in November 2026, so harmonisation matters more than ever.

What is the intended impact?

To stop false trends from shaping fire decisions. A sensor change can make fire activity look several times worse, or hide a real increase. Fire Pulse gives agencies a consistent historical baseline and a tested first look at the coming season. Our analysis also found that the daytime MODIS/VIIRS factor drifts as the MODIS satellites age while the night-time factor stays stable, so harmonisation should be recalibrated every year rather than fixed once.

What tools did we use?

  • Languages: Python; HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Libraries: pandas and NumPy for data processing; scikit-learn (HistGradientBoostingRegressor with Poisson loss) for machine learning. The web app uses no external libraries; maps and charts are drawn with Canvas and SVG.
  • Data: NASA FIRMS MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m (NOAA-20 for harmonisation, S-NPP 2026 for an independent check); Natural Earth for the coastline.
  • Software: Git and GitHub, GitHub Pages hosting, VS Code. Runs on an ordinary laptop with no special hardware.

How is the project creative?

  • A “false trend” demo: a slider shows what happens when a record switches satellites. Raw data jumps about 4.6×; harmonised data stays steady.
  • A locked forecasting contest: predictions were fingerprinted before the 2026 data was downloaded, so nothing could be tuned after the fact, and the winner was chosen by real NASA data.
  • Honest comparison: we let simple methods compete with machine learning. ML won for harmonisation; a simple median won for forecasting. We report both.
  • One colour scale for all views, so judges and users can see how much “hotter” raw VIIRS looks.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Fair testing: every method was scored on years it never saw, with a second split to rule out luck.
  • Data quality: vegetation fires only; confidence filters; archive and near-real-time files handled separately; duplicates removed.
  • “One satellite, one factor”: VIIRS satellites were never mixed, since combining them creates a new false jump.
  • Sparse data: squares with few detections borrow strength from the national factor.
  • What didn’t work: fire radiative power was tested, but its sensor ratio drifts over time, so we harmonise detection counts. The El Niño analog failed in 2026, and we say so.
  • Sensor health: an independent VIIRS S-NPP check confirmed that 2026’s low activity was real, not MODIS degrading.
  • Uncertainty: forecasts come with 80% ranges sized from real errors.
  • Usability: works on phones and in light and dark mode, with plain-English summaries.
  • Limits: 3 harmonised years and Australia only for now. A detection is a fire pixel, not a whole fire. This is a prototype for exploring patterns, not an operational warning system.
